evidence: Read the staged 191-line shell MyAccessibilityService.kt and all ten collaborator files, then diffed the ported PicapAutoAcceptPolicy against the base shouldAutoAccept block pulled with git show, which matches byte for byte except the tag constant and the context parameter

Grep of every call site of pasteOnly, pasteAndSend, hasTextInput, pendingCloseId, hasScannedInitially, clickNode and MyAccessibilityService across app source to check cross-file navigation, duplicated comments and stale monolith references
Walked the shell wiring lines 49 to 72 and the onAccessibilityEvent body against the class KDoc promise, and checked log tag usage in every new module

findings.location: picap/PicapOfferCloser.kt line 41 pendingCloseId and picap/PicapListAutoclicker.kt line 17 hasScannedInitially, driven from picap/PicapOfferProcessor.kt lines 54 and 128 to 133
findings.claim: Both fields were private in the base monolith and are now internal mutable state owned by one class but written by another. The pendingCloseId declaration keeps its threading note but nothing at the declaration site names PicapOfferProcessor as writer or states the read-then-assign-then-schedule sequence, and hasScannedInitially still carries only the old single-class comment with no mention of the external reset, so the cross-class protocol is only half documented. Verdict versus the prior finding: still WARNING, mildly improved for pendingCloseId, unchanged for hasScannedInitially.
proof_refs: PicapOfferCloser line 41 declares a volatile internal var whose comment lines 39 to 40 describe writing in the event and releasing in the coroutine, while PicapOfferProcessor lines 128 to 133 read it, assign it and only then call scheduleNonCvClose

PicapListAutoclicker line 17 declares internal var hasScannedInitially with only the base comment about the initial list scan, yet PicapOfferProcessor line 54 sets it back to false after a captured order
In the base file both fields were private, declared at lines 109 and 112, and the check, assignment and schedule all happened inside one function

findings.location: picap/PicapOfferProcessor.kt constructor parameter line 22 and local line 40; picap/PicapOfferCloser.kt parameter line 35 and local lines 86 to 87
findings.claim: Both collaborators name their injected window supplier picapWindows and then immediately declare a local val of the same name, so the reader sees a list being invoked and loses the provider for the rest of the function. The shell already calls that lambda picapWindowsProvider, so renaming the parameter would remove the shadowing and match the wiring.
proof_refs: PicapOfferProcessor line 22 declares a private val picapWindows of function type and line 40 assigns a local val picapWindows by invoking it, shadowing the property
PicapOfferCloser line 35 declares the same function-typed parameter and attemptNonCvClose lines 86 to 87 repeats the identical shadowing
MyAccessibilityService line 51 names the same lambda picapWindowsProvider and the PicapOfferCloser KDoc at line 28 documents the parameter as a provider

findings.claim: About a quarter of the shell is diagnostic scaffolding: a twenty-two branch mapping of raw event type integers, the EVENT_DEBUG log line and an unconditional dump of every window for every event, none of which is lifecycle, wiring or routing. The class KDoc at lines 27 to 32 describes this file as a thin shell of lifecycle, per-package routing and the facade, so the decoder and dump would read better behind a small debug helper. This block sat in the same callback before the split, so it is pre-existing.
proof_refs: MyAccessibilityService lines 137 to 161 translate integers such as 2048 and 131072 into names solely to feed the EVENT_DEBUG log at lines 162 to 168, and line 170 dumps the window list for every event of every package
The class KDoc at lines 27 to 32 promises only lifecycle, per-package event routing and the public facade
The identical decoder, log and window dump exist in the base file ending at the logWindows call on base line 208, unchanged by the split

findings.location: MyAccessibilityService.kt lines 74 to 94 versus whatsapp/WhatsAppResponder.kt lines 176 to 178, 208 to 211 and 281 to 283
findings.claim: The three facade methods carry KDoc word for word identical to the WhatsAppResponder methods they delegate to, and neither copy mentions the delegation, so a reader of the shell may assume the behavior is implemented there and the two copies can drift independently. Base had each comment only once next to its implementation, so the duplication is created by the split.
proof_refs: MyAccessibilityService lines 74 to 76, 81 to 84 and 89 to 91 repeat the WhatsAppResponder comments at lines 176 to 178, 208 to 211 and 281 to 283
Each shell method body is a single delegation call to whatsappResponder, for example line 78 and line 86
In the base file every one of the three comments appeared only once beside its code
